newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major hunts votes with Underground sale plan.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major hunts votes with Underground sale plan.

text.p: Britain's Conservative government took a big political risk on Tuesday by announcing plans to privatise London's Underground rail network -- the oldest in the world -- if it wins the coming election.
Prime Minister John Major said the Tube, as it is popularly known, would become a world-class system in private hands.
But the main opposition Labour party condemned the plan as half-baked and vowed to scrap it if it takes office.

The Conservatives are gambling that the prospect of extra investment and improved service under private owners will win them votes in marginal London seats -- even though ministers concede the privatisation will be very hard to sell to the public.

The ruling party, which during 18 years in power has sold off state-run steel, rail, water, gas, electricity, telephone and coal industries, also hopes to reap political capital by exposing Labour's general hostility to privatisation.
In a statement to parliament, Transport Secretary Sir George Young said privatisation was the only way to finance the heavy investment needed to modernise London Underground (LU).
Proceeds from the sale, estimated at up to two billion pounds ($3.28 billion), would be ploughed back into the creaking network.
"The government has concluded that privatisation is the right way forward," Young said.

He hoped that privatisation would lead to core investment of around 750 million pounds a year -- 50 percent more than has been achieved so far in the 1990s -- and that LU's 1.2 billion pound investment backlog would be cleared within five years of privatisation.
"I do not believe that this rate of progress would be possible if LU were to remain in the public sector," he said.
The underground network, some of which dates back to 1865, comprises 248 stations on 11 lines that criss-cross one of Europe's biggest cities and transport 2.7 million people a day.
Last week, LU chiefs complained of massive under-investment from the government and listed hundreds of repair and improvement projects that have been shelved as a result.
Labour leader Tony Blair, whose party holds a commanding lead in opinion polls, denounced the government's plans.
If it wins the election, due by May 22, Labour would keep public control of the Tube while exploring ways to attract private finance.

"Is not the London Underground worth probably 7-13 billion pounds, and isn't the fear of many people that once again a key public service will be sold off at a fraction of its true value so that a few people can make a vastly inflated profit with no guarantee of a proper service for the future?" Blair asked.
His transport spokesman Andrew Smith attacked a "half-baked dogma-driven plan from a government bankrupt of ideas".
Smith said: "This is a privatisation which the people of Britain will throw out at the ballot box -- along with the government which dreamed it up."
Reaction from pressure groups was mixed.
Keith Bill of Save Our Railways said the privatisation last year of British Rail (BR) augured ill for the Tube.
"BR privatisation has led to poor management, high fares, low investment and massive fat cat' profits. The same will happen to London Underground," he said.
But the free-market Adam Smith Institute said privatisation was the only way to generate the investment the Tune needs.

"Whatever the pre-election promises, everyone knows that investment for the Tube ranks well below services like schools, hospitals and pensions on the politicians' priority lists," the think tank said. ($1=.6107 Pound)
